initial_prompt: Can you write me a short story about a dragon who's afraid of heights?

messages.content: Can you write me a short story about a dragon who's afraid of heights?

# The Dragon Who Looked Down

Ember had excellent teeth, adequate fire-breathing abilities, and scales that gleamed respectably in sunlight. By most measures, she was a perfectly functional dragon.

She also couldn't fly higher than a barn roof without vomiting.

"It's *psychological*," her mother insisted, circling overhead while Ember clung to a hill. "Dragons don't get afraid of heights. We're literally built for the sky."

"Tell that to my stomach," Ember muttered.

She'd tried everything. Gradual exposure (she'd made it to treetop level before the world started spinning). Motivational mantras ("I am apex predator, I am terror incarnate"—didn't help). Even breathing exercises, though it was hard to focus on your breath when you were actively trying not to look at how far away the ground was.

The real problem came when the village at the valley's edge started refusing to pay tribute.

"They know you can't reach them," her mother said flatly. "That valley's too deep. You'd have to fly *down* to get there, and down is worse than up for you, isn't it?"

It was. Much worse.

But Ember was tired of being the dragon everyone whispered about. The one whose territory was limited to gentle hills and flat plains.

So she walked.

It took three days to get down the mountain path. The villagers saw her coming—had plenty of time to see her coming—and by the time she arrived, they'd assembled in the square, looking confused.

"You're... walking?" the mayor said.

"I have legs." Ember tried to loom, which was less effective when you were winded from hiking. "You've been withholding tribute."

A long pause.

"We thought you couldn't reach us," a woman said. "We thought we were safe."

"I'm a dragon. I have *fire*. I don't need to fly to be dangerous."

Another pause. Then a child's voice: "Are you really scared of heights?"

Ember could have lied. Could have breathed fire for emphasis. Instead, she sat down—which was itself rather alarming to the villagers, given her size.

"Terrified," she admitted. "Looking down makes me want to die. But I can still walk here every month to collect tribute. And I will. It'll just take me three days each direction, which means I'll be *very* irritable when I arrive, so I suggest you have everything ready."

The mayor considered this. "What if... we brought it up to you? Saved you the trip?"

"I'm listening."

They negotiated. A monthly delivery to the hill. Fair terms on both sides. And in exchange, Ember agreed to deal with a bandit problem they'd been having—because it turned out that being a dragon who used ground-based approaches was actually *terrifying* in its own way. Bandits expected aerial attacks. They didn't expect a dragon to simply walk out of the forest at them.

Her mother never quite approved. "It's undignified," she'd say.

But Ember had a new territory, a working arrangement with three villages, and a reputation as the dragon who didn't need wings to be feared.

Some fears, she'd learned, you don't have to conquer. You just have to work around them.

And keep your feet on the ground.
